overview: Cycladic describes the prehistoric societies of the Aegean islands, famous for marble figures, seafaring and later prosperous towns. These islands shared contacts and crafts without forming one known island-wide kingdom. The map’s 4000 to 1500 BCE span begins before the conventional Early Cycladic period and stops before the end of Cycladic Bronze Age history; its outlines are a cultural envelope.

periods.title: Village roots and Early Cycladic communities
periods.summary: Akrotiri had Neolithic inhabitants before the map begins. Early Bronze Age settlements grew through farming, crafts and maritime exchange.

periods.title: Ports and increasingly complex towns
periods.summary: Middle and early Late Cycladic centres developed close connections with Crete and mainland Greece.

items.text: Early Cycladic homes used stone and clay walls, with floors of packed earth or stone slabs. Roofs combined timber, reeds and clay. Small settlements near anchorages, and later on hillsides, placed families close to fields, animals and the sea. Most wooden furnishings have not survived.

Cereals, pulses, olives, fruit and nuts supplied everyday food, supplemented by fish, shellfish and hunted animals. Sheep, goats, cattle and pigs provided food and other useful materials. Feeding a household meant tending crops and animals as well as watching the water for a catch.

Clay spindle whorls and sewing needles reveal household textile work during the third millennium BCE. Impressions of woven mats remain on the bottoms of pots. A mat that rotted away thousands of years ago can still leave its pattern behind, stamped into someone’s crockery.

Many marble figures originally wore colour. Surviving traces show dark blue or black hair, eyebrows and eyes, with red used for jewellery and decorative patterns. Their pale appearance today can hide an important part of the artist’s work: these sculptures were not always all-white faces staring silently back.

Sculptures show people playing harps and wind instruments, alongside figures drinking or embracing. They offer a glimpse of music and gatherings in the third millennium BCE. The instruments can be recognised, but the tunes have not survived. We cannot responsibly supply an ancient Cycladic playlist.

Pictures of many-oared boats and small lead boat models preserve evidence of early island navigation. Obsidian, marble and metals circulated across the Aegean. The water between islands could connect workshops and communities, even when carrying a heavy load required a demanding sea journey.

sections.title: A busy building site and a later town

items.text: At Dhaskalio beside Keros, third-millennium builders created terraces and substantial structures using stone brought from Naxos, about ten kilometres away. Stairs and drainage were planned into the buildings. Transporting the stone itself was a major achievement before a wall could even begin to rise.

Burnt plant remains at Dhaskalio include pulses, grapes, olives, figs, almonds, emmer wheat and barley. The excavators thought Keros probably could not supply all its own food, so boats may have carried provisions as well as prestigious objects. Feeding a busy settlement depended on its wider connections.

The excavators reported five metalworking hearths at Dhaskalio, alongside moulds, crucibles, blowpipes and copper spills. Craftspeople shaped metal through heat and carefully controlled equipment. These finds preserve the tools and mess of production, not just the polished objects that eventually left the workshop.

Much later, at Akrotiri on Thera, paved streets covered a drainage network, and sanitary rooms inside buildings connected directly to it. This was a densely built town with multistorey houses and public buildings. Plumbing had become part of urban planning long before modern bathrooms.

Volcanic deposits at Akrotiri preserved the shapes of wooden furnishings after the wood decayed. Archaeologists could make plaster casts from those empty spaces. Household equipment, bronze vessels and tools survive alongside them, allowing researchers to study furniture and chores rather than only monumental buildings.

Akrotiri’s wall paintings include fishermen, boys and saffron gatherers. The museum reconstructs complete arrangements from the West House and Xesti 3, so figures can be understood within their rooms. These carefully composed pictures reveal what painters chose to show; they are not candid photographs of every family’s day.

The early communities that made the famous marble figures left no written accounts known to the museum’s educational survey. By the later Bronze Age, Akrotiri used Linear A. That script remains undeciphered, so a fluent translation of an islander’s sentence would be guesswork.

A broken pot sherd catalogued as 2839 carries Linear A signs and quantities. One is “𐘎”, shown here in a modern standardised form called AB20, followed on the sherd by the number nine. The quantity is readable; what the sign counts is uncertain. The exact findspot was not recorded, though Akrotiri is considered its likely source.

The inscription was scratched into the pot after firing, when it was probably already a fragment. A piece of broken crockery had become a writing surface. Michailidou places this note most probably in the final occupation period before Akrotiri’s burial by the eruption, rather than in the much earlier age of marble figurines.

ending.text: The eruption buried Akrotiri, but it did not end all Cycladic communities. The map stops at 1500 BCE; later island centres became closely integrated into the Mycenaean world. Cycladic Bronze Age history continues to about 1100 BCE in the National Archaeological Museum’s chronology.
